Yes. This one has **much better raw material than the otter draft**, and I think it could become a really strong page. The kingfisher is inherently theatrical: huge head, absurd bill, rattling call, plunge-diving, fish-smacking, burrow digging. We do **not** need to make it sound important. We just need to get out of the bird’s way.

My overall reaction: **keep the female-more-colorful fact, the rattle, the dive, the fish-smacking, the burrow, and the park photographer connection. Cut or rewrite most of the generic “food chain / territory / habitat management” material.** A few claims also need correction or softening.

The best opening is already sitting there:

> The female Belted Kingfisher is more colorful than the male.

That is immediately interesting. I would probably make it even more conversational:

> **Here, the female gets the extra color.** Both sexes wear a blue-gray band across the chest, but the female adds a rusty band across her belly.

That is cleaner than “a genuine reversal of the usual pattern in North American birds.” The reversal is real and unusual, but the present wording sounds like a bird guide trying to impress me. Cornell specifically notes that females are more colorful than males because of that chestnut belly band. ([All About Birds][1])

The second Quick Hit is excellent:

> You will probably hear it before you see it...

Keep that. That is **exactly** the kind of thing a person at the park can use five minutes later. Cornell uses essentially the same field advice: the loud rattling call often gives the bird away first. ([All About Birds][2])

events.notes:
Much better. **This now feels like a page I’d actually want to read at the pond.** The academic sludge is mostly gone, the best facts are up front, and the bird’s behavior is doing the work.

I’d still make a handful of changes.

The **first three At a Glance items are strong**. I’d keep them almost exactly as written. The female-more-colorful fact is both true and genuinely unusual, and “nobody is entirely sure why” is supported. Cornell specifically discusses competing hypotheses without a settled answer. ([All About Birds][1])

The fourth At a Glance item is the weakest of the four:

> We can see them year-round, but fall and winter bring more of them south as birds from farther up the continent push toward open water.

The underlying migration story is right: some Belted Kingfishers stay where water remains open, while northern birds migrate south. ([All About Birds][2]) But “we can see them year-round” sounds like **park-specific evidence**. If that comes from your actual observations, great. If not, I’d soften it to:

> **Some stay in Florida year-round, while fall and winter bring additional birds south from colder parts of the continent.**

That is cleaner and avoids implying your park has documented year-round presence unless it has.

## How to know it

This is substantially improved.

I do think **five blocks is still one too many**. “Size and shape” and “What to look for” partly overlap.

I’d probably combine them.

Something like:

**Size and shape**

> About thirteen inches long — roughly robin-sized, but built nothing like one. The oversized head, shaggy crest and thick dagger-like bill give it a top-heavy look. Look for that silhouette perched above open water, or hovering bill-down before a dive.

Then keep:

* Markings
* In flight
* Voice

That gives you four blocks.

The **white wing patch is a very good addition**. Cornell explicitly points to the large white patch in the outer wing as an in-flight clue. ([All About Birds][3])
